evidence: The CI pipeline runs an automated test suite on changes before they merge or deploy
expected_output: One observation row with workflow_count and test_step_count

assertions.description: At least one workflow step runs a recognized test command — changes are tested, not just built.

caveats: Recognizes common test invocations by pattern; a bespoke test harness under an unrecognized name reads as absent.
notes: Empty-set discipline — Counter: repo-facts always emits exactly one summary row of workflow and test-step counts, so a repo with no CI at all violates honestly instead of passing over an empty set; an empty observation set here could only mean the collector never ran.

plain.checks: Reads the CI workflows and looks for a step that actually runs a test suite, rather than only building, installing or linting.
plain.violation: Changes reach the default branch with nothing checking that they work. Every other control that rests on “the pipeline would have caught it” is resting on a pipeline that does not look.
plain.fix: Add a test step to the workflow that runs on pull requests, and require it to pass before merge. A suite that runs only on a developer's machine is not part of the pipeline.

upstream_overlap.note: SA-11 asks for developer testing AND evaluation, and this pairing splits on that word. Upstream's recipe is entirely about the evaluation limb — static analysis configured, scoped, scheduled and dispositioned. This one is about the testing limb: a workflow step runs a recognised test command, so changes are tested before they merge rather than only built. The two are complementary rather than competing, and the overlap is declared rather than left implicit because a reader seeing one control id on two catalogs has no way to tell a split limb from a duplicated claim. What this recipe does not establish, and their route does, is that the testing reaches every repository in the boundary — this is one checkout's workflow file, and the repository set is named by a human.
